meta.title: Office Ergonomics
meta.description: Learn how to set up an ergonomic workstation, recognize office injury risks, and adopt safe work habits to prevent musculoskeletal disorders.

lessons.ergonomics-overview:
**Understanding Office Ergonomics**

Ergonomics is the study of how the things we use can be designed, arranged, and adjusted to fit us better. In the office, ergonomics helps employees work more safely, comfortably, and efficiently. Poor workstation setup, repetitive motion, and awkward postures can lead to musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) such as carpal tunnel syndrome, tendinitis, neck strain, and lower back pain. These injuries often develop gradually rather than from a single event. The goal of ergonomics is to make the workplace fit the worker instead of forcing the worker to fit the workplace.

• Ergonomics adapts the job, tools, and workstation to the worker.
• Poor setup can cause discomfort, fatigue, pain, and injury over time.
• Office injuries often develop gradually from repeated small stresses.
• Ergonomic improvements increase comfort, productivity, and safety.
lessons.office-injury-risks:
**Office Injury Risks**

Ergonomic injuries occur when muscles, tendons, ligaments, nerves, or joints are placed under more stress than they can safely handle. Common office risk factors include repetitive motion (typing, clicking, reaching), awkward postures (bent wrists, raised shoulders, forward lean), excessive force (forcing a stapler), poor workstation design, and lack of movement. Common MSDs include carpal tunnel syndrome (pressure on the median nerve causing numbness or tingling), tendinitis (inflamed tendons), lower back pain from poor lumbar support, and neck or shoulder strain from poor monitor placement or phone cradling.

• Repetitive motion is one of the most common office ergonomic risk factors.
• Awkward postures increase physical stress on muscles and joints.
• Excessive force when using office tools raises injury risk.
• MSDs include carpal tunnel syndrome, tendinitis, lower back pain, and neck strain.
lessons.workspace-organization:
**Workspace Organization**

How your desk is organized directly affects your ergonomic risk. Frequently used items should be kept about 14 to 18 inches away to prevent overreaching and twisting. Items used less often can be placed farther away. Phones deserve special attention: cradling the phone between the head and shoulder strains the neck and upper back. A headset or speakerphone keeps the neck in a more neutral position. Office tools such as staplers and paper cutters should never be forced beyond their design limits. Use a heavy-duty stapler for large stacks and make smaller cuts rather than overloading a paper cutter.

• Keep frequently used items 14 to 18 inches away to reduce reaching.
• Use a headset or speakerphone to avoid neck strain from phone cradling.
• Never force office tools beyond their intended capacity.
• Select the right tool for the job to reduce excessive force.
lessons.neutral-posture-chair-setup:
**Neutral Posture and Chair Setup**

A neutral position is a comfortable posture where joints are naturally aligned and muscles do not have to work hard to hold the position. Proper chair setup is the foundation of a neutral posture. Adjust chair height so forearms rest comfortably at the work surface with elbows at about 90 to 120 degrees. Thighs should be roughly parallel to the floor, knees near hip height, and feet fully supported. The chair back should support the natural forward curve of the lower back (lumbar support). If feet do not reach the floor flat, use a footrest to reduce stress on the spine. Keep shoulders relaxed and avoid sitting on the front edge of the chair.

• Neutral posture keeps joints naturally aligned to reduce muscle strain.
• Adjust chair height so elbows form a 90 to 120 degree angle at the work surface.
• Use lumbar support to maintain the natural curve of the lower back.
• Use a footrest if feet do not rest flat on the floor after chair adjustment.
lessons.computer-workstation-setup:
**Computer Workstation Setup**

Proper placement of the keyboard, mouse, monitor, and documents reduces wrist, arm, shoulder, neck, and eye strain. Keep wrists flat and straight while typing; avoid bending them up, down, or sideways. Place the mouse close to the keyboard and move the whole arm when using it rather than only the wrist. The monitor should be about 16 to 27 inches from the eyes at a comfortable viewing angle that allows a slight downward gaze. A monitor placed too high causes neck extension; too low causes forward bending. Use a document holder to keep reference materials near the monitor and reduce repeated neck movement and eye refocusing.

• Keep wrists flat and straight while typing to reduce pressure on the median nerve.
• Place the mouse close to the keyboard; move the whole arm, not just the wrist.
• Position the monitor 16 to 27 inches away with a slight downward viewing angle.
• Use a document holder to reduce repeated head movement during data entry.
lessons.movement-stretching:
**Movement, Stretching, and Micro-Breaks**

Even the best workstation cannot protect you if you remain in one position all day. The body is designed for movement. Changing position, standing briefly, walking, and stretching reduce uneven stresses that can lead to pain and injury. Recommended stretches include: hand and wrist stretches (make fists then spread fingers; gently stretch fingers back), neck stretches (slowly turn head side to side), shoulder stretches and rolls, and lower back relief (sit up and slowly bend forward toward the knees). Practical movement tips include standing during phone calls, walking to speak with coworkers, and taking brief posture breaks during long computer tasks.

• Sitting still for long periods creates fatigue and cumulative strain.
• Micro-breaks and position changes reduce physical stress throughout the day.
• Gentle stretching of hands, wrists, neck, shoulders, and back reduces tension.
• A properly set up workstation does not eliminate the need for movement.
lessons.health-wellness-stress:
**Health, Wellness, and Stress Reduction**

Overall health affects how the body responds to physical stress at work. Workplace stress increases muscle tension, which can contribute to discomfort and injury risk. Deep breathing exercises help reduce tension during the workday. Regular aerobic activity (walking, cycling, jogging) strengthens the body, supports cardiovascular health, and reduces stress. Healthy eating, staying hydrated, getting adequate rest, and avoiding harmful habits all support a safer work life. Employees should report persistent pain, numbness, or tingling early. Employers are responsible for providing ergonomics training, evaluating workstation concerns, and providing appropriate equipment such as headsets, footrests, and monitor risers.

• Stress increases muscle tension and can raise ergonomic injury risk.
• Deep breathing and relaxation exercises reduce tension during the workday.
• Employees should report discomfort early before symptoms become serious.
• Employers must provide training, evaluate concerns, and supply ergonomic equipment.

1.questionText: The primary goal of ergonomics in the workplace is to:

options.text: Increase production speed at all costs
Ensure tools, workstations, and tasks are adapted to fit the worker
Remove all furniture from the office
Replace hands-on training with video only

2.questionText: Ergonomic injuries in the office can result from which combination of factors?

options.text: Repetitive motion, awkward posture, and excessive force

3.questionText: Which statement best describes a neutral working position?

options.text: Joints naturally aligned with minimal muscle effort
Sitting on the front edge of the chair

4.questionText: True or False: Holding a phone between the head and shoulder is a safe practice that does not stress the neck.

5.questionText: To prevent overreaching and strain, frequently used items should be positioned approximately:

options.text: On a separate table behind the worker
About 14 to 18 inches away, within easy reach

6.questionText: After adjusting your chair height, your feet do not reach the floor flat. The correct next step is to:

options.text: Place stacked books under your feet
Accept the discomfort and continue working

7.questionText: To reduce the risk of wrist injury while typing, the keyboard should be positioned so that your wrists are:

8.questionText: Which mouse placement best supports neutral posture and reduces shoulder strain?

options.text: On the opposite side of the desk from the keyboard
On a surface far below the keyboard
Close to the keyboard, within easy reach
As far from the keyboard as possible

9.questionText: Using a document holder during data entry primarily helps by:

options.text: Increasing the brightness of the screen
Keeping a backup copy of your work
Reducing repeated neck movement and eye refocusing

10.questionText: True or False: Once a workstation is set up with ergonomic adjustments, the employee no longer needs to change positions or take movement breaks.

11.questionText: A worker types for hours each day and develops tingling in the fingers. The wrists are consistently bent upward. The most appropriate immediate action is to:

options.text: Correct the wrist position by adjusting the keyboard or chair and report the discomfort
Increase typing speed to finish faster
Move the keyboard to a different workstation

12.questionText: An employee has to press very hard on a standard stapler to staple thick packets of paper. What is the safest ergonomic correction?

options.text: Have the employee use both hands for more force
Use the edge of the stapler instead
Replace it with a heavy-duty stapler built for larger volumes
Staple only one page at a time

13.questionText: A monitor is positioned too low, causing an employee to bend the neck forward for hours each day. What injury risk is most likely?

14.questionText: True or False: Waiting until ergonomic discomfort becomes severe before reporting it is an acceptable practice.

15.questionText: Which of the following actions falls within the employer's ergonomic responsibilities?

options.text: Telling employees to work through discomfort
Evaluating workstation concerns and providing ergonomic equipment when needed
Ignoring reported discomfort if no injury has occurred
